title: SLO-aware burst throttle playbook (draft)
summary: Working draft: an SRE playbook for detecting and mitigating short-duration traffic bursts that cause dedicated GPU pool SLO degradation. Focused on dynamic throttle policies, rapid isolation, and safe autoscaler interaction.
body:
Context

Problem statement: we keep seeing short (1–10 minute) traffic bursts from a small number of tenants that cause local queueing on dedicated GPU pools. Symptoms: percentiles (p95/p99) for model latency spike by 2–8x, token throughput falls for adjacent tenants, autoscaler either over-reacts (mass scale-up) or under-reacts (no change), and eviction cascades sometimes follow. Existing runbooks focus on long-lived noisy tenants; this playbook aims to handle short bursts without inducing expensive scale events or noisy evictions.

Why this matters
- Customer SLOs (p99 <= X ms) are violated during bursts; incidents increase noise and alert fatigue.
- Reactive autoscaler activity increases cost and can destabilize pools.
- Current noisy-tenant heuristics rely on longer observation windows; short bursts slip through.

Signals to watch (dashboards/metrics)
- pool.request_rate_per_gpu: sudden per-GPU request rate jump > 3x baseline in 30s
- pool.pending_queue_length: > 30 requests queued per instance for > 60s
- pool.kernel_utilization_pct: short spikes > 85% across a subset of GPUs
- tenant.request_burstiness: rolling-window CV (coefficient of variation) for requests > 1.5
- autoscaler.actions: spike in scale events correlated within 2m of burst start
- kv_cache_miss_ratio: elevated misses during bursts (implies prefix reuse drop)
- p99_latency_by_tenant and p99_latency_by_pool: identify who is suffering vs who is causing

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes)
1) Acknowledge alert and note start time.
2) Look at p99_latency_by_pool and p99_latency_by_tenant dashboards. Identify top 3 tenants contributing to pool load.
3) Correlate with autoscaler logs: any scale ops in last 5 minutes? If yes, annotate.
4) Check allocation spread: are requests concentrated on a small set of GPUs? (hot-shard)
5) Inspect recent commits/rollouts in the last hour (Console -> rollouts) to rule out regressions.
6) If bursting tenant(s) are obvious and non-critical, consider immediate temporary request throttling (see throttle options).

Containment tactics (safe, minimal blast radius)
- Dynamic short-window throttle: apply a token-bucket style rate limit to tenant(s) for 60–300s with a soft drop. Prefer 'throttle-with-backoff' over hard evictions. Implementation step: use per-tenant ingress limiter service to add a 1m token bucket at 50–70% of recent baseline.
- Route-splitting: divert a copy of offending tenant traffic to a low-cost compatibility model or a non-SLA pool (if configured) until burst subsides.
- Prefixed KV warming: if kv_cache_miss_ratio is high, trigger warmup jobs (best-effort) for top request prefixes to reduce load.
- Localized niceness: if we see hot-shard, shift ephemeral jobs off the affected GPUs using allocator isolate operation (best-effort, not for heavy production).

When to evict (and when not to)
- Eviction is last-resort for persistent noisy tenants (> 10m sustained high queueing despite throttles). Evict only if: clear evidence of one tenant consuming > 60% of pool queue slots AND throttles/backoffs failed.
- Avoid eviction during short bursts unless the tenant is exceeding contract or DoS-like traffic. Eviction causes churn and may trigger autoscaler ripples.

Autoscaler interaction guidance
- Autoscaler windowing: temporarily extend autoscaler aggregation window by 60–120s when a burst is active to avoid immediate scale-up. Add a short hysteresis flag to prevent flip-flop.
- Scale-up gating: require two consecutive 60s windows of sustained utilization > threshold before autoscaler ups the pool.
- Emergency burst policy: enable a 'burst-burst' tier — short-lived best-effort capacity that can be spawned from a lower-cost instance class for up to 5 minutes without impacting tenant placement. (Design note: requires infra changes; tracked in JIRA-ENG-8742)

Commands / console steps (cheat sheet)
- Identify top tenants: console -> metrics -> p99_latency_by_tenant (filter pool=POOL_ID, last 15m)
- Apply token-bucket throttle: cli control-plane throttle set --tenant TENANT_ID --policy burst-short --duration 120s --rate 60rps
- Temporarily mark tenant lower-priority: allocator annotate-tenancy TENANT_ID priority=degraded-comment
- Trigger warmup job: infra job run kv-warmup --pool POOL_ID --prefixes-file /tmp/pfxs.txt
- Extend autoscaler window: autoscaler tweak --pool POOL_ID --window-sec 120 --hysteresis 30s

Post-incident notes (what to capture before handover)
- Start/end wall-clock times and duration of elevated p99s.
- Tenants implicated and their request signatures (endpoints, prompt sizes, burst pattern).
- Exact throttles or actions taken (CLI commands, console changes).
- Autoscaler actions in same timeframe.
- Any downstream fallout (evictions, re-balances, failed jobs).
- Quick boolean: Was traffic legitimate (customer campaign) or anomalous?

Hypotheses and experiments (open items)
1) Hypothesis: short bursts are primarily caused by client-side retry storms after small transient errors. Experiment: add synthetic jitter/backoff recommendations to SDK and instrument client-side retry patterns.
2) Hypothesis: model switchovers (rollouts) cause temporary cache/kv thrashing leading to higher GPU kernel loads. Experiment: tie rollouts to a warmup period with traffic shadowing.
3) Hypothesis: autoscaler reacts too quickly to surface utilization spikes. Experiment: run a canary with increased autoscaler window on 2 pools for 2 weeks.

Runbook improvements to implement
- Add 'burst' alert type with explicit SLO violation window and automated soft throttle API trigger.
- Enhance dashboards with tenant burstiness heatmap and short-window queue summaries.
- Implement a safe ephemeral slab for short bursts (burst-burst tier) to accept overflow without touching main pool.
- Automated post-incident template (populate summary, tenant list, commands executed).

On-call notes from last 2025-09-02 event (raw)
- 21:12: alert p99 pool-nyc-3 rose to 2.7x baseline. Noticed sudden jog in request_rate on tenant T-2317.
- 21:14: applied 120s throttle at 50rps via cli. p99 dropped to 1.2x after ~40s.
- 21:17: autoscaler attempted one scale-up. We extended window to 120s; scale action aborted.
- 21:21: kv_cache_miss_ratio peaked — triggered warmup job (manual).
- 21:30: normalised. No eviction performed. Logged JIRA-INC-5621 for follow-up.

Pending action items (owners)
- Aisha: implement small API to apply per-tenant soft-throttles and audit trail (due 2025-10-01).
- Liam: prototype burst-burst ephemeral slab in allocator (POC branch in repo, due 2025-09-18).
- Rocio: update dashboards with burstiness heatmap (due 2025-09-12).
- Samir: run autoscaler-window canary on two pools (start 2025-09-07).

Questions for PM/Infra
- Is a low-cost ephemeral slab acceptable from a billing/commit perspective for customers? (billing/contract implications)
- Can we introduce an API-level soft-throttle that customers can opt-in to for graceful degradation?

Notes to self
- Keep throttles conservative: false positives cause customer complaints. Prefer short soft-throttles and rapid rollback.
- Document clear customer communication template for when we apply soft throttles.

Appendix: quick glossary
- burst-burst slab: ephemeral short-lived capacity intended to absorb short spikes without rebalancing main pool.
- token-bucket short throttle: soft limit that allows occasional bursts above baseline but reduces sustained peak.
- kv warmup: proactively populate model KV/cache prefixes expected in the next minutes to reduce cache-miss pressure.

End of draft.

Feedback welcome — this is intended as an operationally actionable draft for the SRE on-call to use during short burst incidents on dedicated pools.
